edges.description: The blunted lipolytic signal was associated with excess triglyceride in peripheral adipose tissue; the causal chain was proposed rather than demonstrated.
edges.source: Blunted Catecholamine-Stimulated Adenylate Cyclase Activation in Peripheral Adipose Tissue

nodes.description: In peripheral subcutaneous adipose tissue from the reported children, noradrenaline poorly stimulated adenylate cyclase and isoprenaline produced no rise in tissue cyclic AMP, with correspondingly impaired glycerol release. The historical authors placed the defect at or before cyclic-AMP generation, in contrast to the preserved-cAMP type 2 pattern, but neither the affected protein nor the precise step was identified, and the assay was performed on tissue from severely malnourished children.
nodes.id: Blunted Catecholamine-Stimulated Adenylate Cyclase Activation in Peripheral Adipose Tissue

biological_processes: adenylate cyclase-activating adrenergic receptor signaling pathway

evidence.reference_title: Triglyceride storage disease. A report of two affected children associated with neurological abnormalities.
evidence.snippet: Peripheral adipose tissue of one of these children displayed: (a) reduced sensitivity of adenyl cyclase to stimulation by noradrenaline (b) no response in tissue levels of cyclic AMP when stimulated by isoprenaline and (c) impaired release of glycerol following stimulation with isoprenaline.
In one infant noradrenaline(10−5M) poorly stimulated the activity of adenyl cyclase in subcutaneous adipose tissue in the periphery compared to abdominal tissue (P < 0.05)

nodes.description: Triglyceride deposits persisted in peripheral adipose tissue despite severe malnutrition. The authors postulated a primary adipose-tissue defect that interferes with triglyceride mobilization during prolonged malnutrition.

evidence.reference_title: Triglyceride storage disease. A report of two affected children associated with neurological abnormalities.
evidence.snippet: It is postulated that a primary metabolic defect occurs in peripheral adipose tissue (and possibly at other sites such as the liver) that interferes with triglyceride (and glycogen) mobilization during prolonged malnutrition.
